Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 124 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 124 (Whitla 
WMU) includes part of the city of Medicine Hat and the 
surrounding area to the west. The boundaries of WMU 
124 are defined by highways and roads. The WMU 
starts at the junction of Highways 1 and 3 in Medicine 
Hat, then runs northwest along Highway 1 to Range 
Road 9-3. The boundary then runs south along Range 
Road 9-3 to Secondary Highway 524. The boundary 
then runs west along Secondary Road 524 to 
Secondary Road 879, then south along Secondary 
Road 879 to Highway 3, then northeast along Highway 
3 to the starting point. The WMU is relatively small with 
an area of 1468 km2. WMU 124 is bisected by the 
South Saskatchewan River which is oriented mainly in 
an east/west direction. Approximately 75 percent of 
the WMU is heavily impacted by human development 
including annual cultivation (both dryland and 
irrigation), wind farm development, and road networks. 
The remaining 25 percent is native grassland, mainly 
associated with the river valley.  Most of the remaining 
mule deer habitat in the WMU is associated with the 
coulees and draws along the South Saskatchewan 
River. 
Chronic Wasting Disease is now well established 
within the WMU, with 56 positives since first detected 
in 2017 (https://open.alberta.ca/publications/chronic-
wasting-disease-in-alberta-by-wildlife-management-
unit) . Submitted samples from 2023 indicate 
prevalence rates of 24% in mule deer and 40% of 15 
mule deer bucks tested positive for the disease. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer) 
was last conducted for WMU 124 in 2009 using the 
modified Gassaway/random stratified block 
methodology (Table 1). With over 15 years since the 
last survey, an updated population estimate is needed 
to ensure management is based on more relevant 
data. It is important to consider the difference in 
methods when comparing results between the 
surveys.  
T
he objective of the February 2025 survey was to 
assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 
124 by determining estimates for abundance, density 
and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including 
moose, pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and 
sensitive or at-risk species. 
Survey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 11, 2025, flying 27 east-west lines 
at 1.85 km intervals, with 50% coverage (800 m wide 
survey strip, area surveyed 729 km2) for a total linear 
survey effort of 912 km. At each observation point, 
ungulates were classified by species, and when 
possible, sex and age were recorded. Antler size for 
deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on 
one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more 
points; antlers inside ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 
points, antlers outside of ears). Snow conditions in 
February of 2025 were excellent with near 100% 
coverage. This provided maximum visibility to detect 
ungulates during the survey.  
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer and white-tailed deer, was 
calculated by multiplying the number of animals per 
transect (∑x) by total area (km2) searched (total 
survey strip area [∑z]) (Jolly 1969, as described in 
Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area (km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine 
population estimates with 90% confidence intervals. 
Confidence interval width was calculated by 
multiplying the t statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the 
Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard 
error (SE; without replacement) of the abundance 
estimate where SE=sq root variance, and 
variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) 
with N as the total number of possible transects given 
100% coverage, and n as the number of transects 
sampled. 
Moose observations made during the survey were also 
recorded, however small numbers of animals seen 
were not conducive to estimating a population for the 
WMU.

Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 223 mule deer were observed with an 
average groups size of 7 (range 1-28). The estimated 
density was 0.31 mule deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 449 individuals (90% CI 287 – 611). A 
total of 219 mule deer were successfully classified and 
the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 
16:100:78. That results in an estimated 2025 winter 
mule deer population of 37 bucks, 232 does, and 180 
fawns. Of the 18 mule deer bucks classified, 13 (72%) 
were classified ‘small’, 2 (11%) ‘medium’, and 3 (17%) 
‘large’. The 2025 population estimate represents a 
37% decrease from the last aerial ungulate survey 
population estimate for mule deer within WMU 124 
(conducted in 2009). The 2009 survey did not provide 
data on buck to doe and fawn to doe ratios so a 
comparison cannot be made (Table 1). When 
comparing survey results, it is important to note that 
the last survey used a different survey methodology 
(modified Gassaway/random block). Furthermore, the 
low buck to doe ratio in 2025 is undoubtedly an artifact 
of significant antler drop occurring prior to the survey. 
Surveyors did observe bucks with only one antler, as 
well as large-bodied animals that exhibited 
characteristics of buck with no antlers. 
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 265 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 20 (range 2-59). The estimated 
density was 0.36 deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 533 individuals (90% CI (219-848). 
Only three white-tailed bucks were observed on the 
survey, indicating that antler drop was almost 
completed. Due to this fact, buck, doe, and fawn 
classification was not possible. The 2025 population 
estimate represents a 67% increase when compared 
to 2009 data, however once again different 
methodologies were used between surveys, so results 
are not directly comparable.  
Incidental observations 
A total of two moose were observed consisting of a 
cow/calf unit. Moose habitat is limited in this WMU, 
and they are generally confined to brushy coulees 
along the South Saskatchewan river.    
An estimated total of 285 pronghorn were observed 
during the survey. Other species observed included 
gray partridge, coyote, and red fox.
